articles.title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing Appoints New Chair
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing reports significant progress in rehousing residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, with over 600 homes now vacant following safety concerns.
articles.content_html:
More than 600 homes are currently empty in Rochdale following the decision by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) to evict the remaining residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, officially known as College Bank. This decision was announced in October 2025 and has led to a significant reduction in the number of households living in the area, with only around 100 households still awaiting relocation out of approximately 760 total flats.

The eviction process, which was initially met with shock by residents, was clarified by RBH to take place over an 18-month period. As of late August 2026, 117 households have accepted offers for new accommodation, with 82 having already moved and a further 35 in the process of relocating. The remaining residents are primarily those who have not yet found suitable housing, as many have left due to what RBH describes as 'natural attrition', which includes reasons such as tenancy endings or voluntary departures.

The need for these evictions arose from safety concerns identified in a recent building survey. The survey highlighted various issues, including structural and electrical problems, water pumping system failures, roof damage, and rising costs for heating and lighting. RBH has stated that all tenants will receive support during their transition to new homes, including financial assistance for those affected. Leaseholders will have their properties purchased at market value.

This situation has been ongoing for nearly a decade, with plans for the demolition of some of the high-rises initially proposed in 2017. Although demolition was ruled out in 2023, RBH has since reopened discussions about the future of the tower blocks, stating that no final decision has been made regarding potential demolition. Local campaigners from the Save the Seven Sisters group have expressed concerns about the implications of these developments, fearing that the evictions may lead to a permanent loss of housing in the area.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Late-Night Car Wash Proposal on Kingsway
articles.excerpt: A proposed late-night car wash on Kingsway has been refused by Rochdale Council following concerns from local residents about noise and traffic impact.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has unanimously rejected a proposal for a late-night car wash on Kingsway, following significant concerns from local residents regarding noise and traffic impact. The application, submitted by Moonbeam Car Wash, sought to establish five self-service jet wash bays, alongside a laundrette pod, a dog wash pod, and a vending machine, on the site of the former Paul Price Cars dealership.

During a planning committee meeting on September 2, residents expressed their worries about the potential disruption caused by the car wash's operating hours, which were proposed to be from 8am to 11pm. A representative from the Merinall Close residents highlighted that the area already suffers from parking issues, stating, "Residents already experience vehicles parking outside the site. We have evidence of real world conditions being in this area."

Councillor Shakil Ahmed questioned how the developer could justify the operation of the car wash without supervision, while Matthew Gray, representing Moonbeam, claimed that a noise impact assessment had been accepted by Environmental Health. He noted that the original proposal for a 24-hour operation had been reduced to the current hours in response to community concerns, and that measures such as fencing and planting would be implemented to mitigate noise.

Despite these assurances, Councillor Sameena Zaheer raised concerns about the additional traffic on Kingsway, stating, "Most of the time Kingsway is a packed road. It is going to add more to this." The planning committee ultimately decided to refuse the application, citing noise, traffic impact, and the effect on residential amenity as key factors in their decision.

articles.title: Tram Services Suspended Between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre This Saturday
articles.excerpt: No trams will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre until 2pm on Saturday, with further service changes expected on Sunday due to maintenance works.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that there will be no tram services operating between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre this Saturday until 2pm. This disruption is part of ongoing maintenance and improvement works on the network.

Additionally, on Sunday, tram services will be affected from the start of service until 11am due to works at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar. Passengers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as these changes may lead to delays and altered service patterns across the network.

TfGM is also addressing accessibility issues at several tram stops. The lift at Derker tram stop is currently out of service, and passengers travelling towards Manchester can use a ramp from Cromford Street to access the platform. For those heading away from Manchester, a ramp and track crossing are available for access to the Rochdale bound platform.

At Failsworth tram stop, both lifts are out of service while replacement works are carried out. Passengers requiring step-free access are advised to travel to Hollinwood to connect with services. For further assistance, customers can contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000, available from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends.

articles.content_html:
Medieval knights will return to Whitworth this month for Saturday Knight Fights 6, a full-contact Medieval combat event taking place at The Ashcroft on Saturday, September 26. The event is organised by Honour and Arms HMB Ltd, a Rochdale-based independent club dedicated to the study and competition of historical martial arts.

Participants will engage in battles within an MMA-style cage, showcasing their skills in full armour. The event promises an evening filled with excitement and adrenaline as knights go head to head in thrilling showdowns. The organisers stated, 'We keep the action rocking and rolling with Saturday Knight Fights 6.'

Honour and Arms HMB Ltd, owned by Daniel and Mary George, offers workshops and courses on various styles of historical fencing and European martial arts, catering to both beginners and experienced practitioners. The club aims to promote the sport and provide opportunities for enthusiasts to train and compete in full-contact Medieval combat.

Tickets for the event are expected to be in high demand, and attendees are encouraged to secure their places early to witness this unique spectacle of Medieval combat. Further details regarding ticket sales and event timings can be found on the Honour and Arms website.

articles.title: Rochdale Residents Urged to Check Voter Registration Ahead of 2027 Elections
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council reminds residents to verify their electoral registration details to ensure they can vote in the upcoming local elections in May 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is urging residents to check their electoral registration details to avoid losing their chance to vote in the local elections scheduled for May 2027. The council's annual canvass aims to keep the electoral register up to date and identify individuals who may be at risk of not being registered in time for the elections.

Edward McCreadie, elections manager at Rochdale Borough Council, stated that over the summer, emails were sent to residents in more than 40,000 properties, asking them to verify their details. Follow-up letters were dispatched this week, and residents are encouraged to keep an eye out for these communications. McCreadie emphasised the importance of ensuring that the information on the electoral register is accurate and up to date, saying, "To make sure you don’t lose your say at upcoming elections, simply follow the instructions sent to you."

Residents who have recently moved homes are particularly urged to check their registration status. Research from the Electoral Commission indicates that recent movers are less likely to be registered compared to those who have lived at the same address for a longer period. In Great Britain, 92% of individuals who have lived in their home for 16 years are registered, while only 36% of those who have lived at an address for less than a year are registered.

Individuals aged 16 and above can be added to the electoral register, although they will not be eligible to vote until they turn 18. For those wishing to register, the easiest method is through the Rochdale Borough Council website at rochdale.gov.uk/RegisterToVote. Ensuring that your registration is current is crucial for participating in the democratic process.

articles.title: Prime Minister Calls for Accountability in Michael Hoolickin Murder Case
articles.excerpt: The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in Middleton in 2016, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding the probation system that failed to protect him.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

17:42, 03 September 2026

The family of murdered Middleton resident Michael Hoolickin has expressed support for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding failures in the probation system that contributed to his death.

17:18, 03 September 2026

The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in Middleton in 2016, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding the probation system that failed to protect him.

The family of Michael Hoolickin, a 27-year-old father murdered in Middleton in 2016, has expressed support for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent call for accountability in the probation system. This follows the tragic circumstances surrounding Michael's death, which his family believes were exacerbated by failures within the system.

Michael was killed by an offender who had a history of violent crime, including a previous conviction for biting off a man's ear. Despite over 50 breaches of his probation licence, including positive drug tests and arrests, he remained free until he fatally stabbed Michael outside the Friendship Inn on Cheapside on October 14, 2016.

In Parliament, Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell highlighted the need for reform, stating that the local Probation Service should have acted more decisively to monitor the offender. The Hoolickin family, alongside other victims' families, has co-founded the campaign group VOICE (Victims Oversight In Criminal Enforcement) to advocate for changes in the probation system and to seek a formal apology from the Government for the failures that led to such tragedies.

The Prime Minister's remarks have reignited discussions about the need for a comprehensive review of the Probation Service, which VOICE claims is responsible for one victim every three days. The Hoolickin family hopes that this renewed focus will lead to meaningful reforms that prevent similar incidents in the future.

articles.excerpt: The British Furniture Association is hosting a health and safety seminar in Rochdale on 30 September, focusing on risks faced by workers in the furniture industry.
articles.content_html:
The British Furniture Association (BFA) has announced a health and safety seminar titled 'Behind the Mask', which will take place at Rochdale Occupational Health Services (ROHS) on Wednesday, 30 September. This event aims to address specific risks faced by workers in the furniture industry and is designed for business owners, health and safety managers, and anyone responsible for personal protective equipment (PPE) and compliance with the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH).

The seminar will feature expert-led presentations, live face-fit testing, and workshops covering topics such as hearing and respiratory risks, stress in the workplace, and PPE provision. Phil Spademan, Managing Director of the BFA, emphasised the importance of providing meaningful and relevant training to members, stating that the seminar combines practical experience with expert insights to support legislative compliance.

Helen Yates, General Manager at ROHS, highlighted the significance of events like this, noting that they prioritise the well-being of employees and equip employers with the necessary tools to protect their workforce effectively. The seminar is open to BFA members and clients of ROHS, ensuring that those in the furniture manufacturing sector can benefit from this tailored training opportunity.

Attendees can expect to gain valuable knowledge and practical skills that can be directly applied in their workplaces, enhancing health and safety standards across the industry. For more information about the event and registration details, interested parties are encouraged to visit the BFA's official website.

articles.title: Five Lamborghinis and a Mercedes Seized Following Dangerous Driving Reports on M66 and M62
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police seized six high-performance vehicles in Rochdale as part of a crackdown on anti-social driving, following reports of dangerous behaviour on the M66.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

13:11, 03 September 2026

Greater Manchester Police seized six high-performance vehicles in Rochdale as part of a crackdown on anti-social driving, following reports of dangerous behaviour on the M66.

Officers from Greater Manchester Police’s Transport Policing and Crime Command (TPACC) seized six luxury cars in Rochdale last night as part of a crackdown on anti-social and dangerous driving. The operation followed reports of reckless driving involving high-powered vehicles, including Lamborghinis and Mercedes G-Wagons, on the M66.

Witnesses reported that the vehicles were being driven at excessive speeds, weaving across lanes, and performing wheel spins, with some slowing down to speeds as low as 17mph on the motorway. Police located the convoy on the M62 and successfully stopped two Lamborghinis as they exited the motorway. The remaining vehicles were brought to a halt using specialist tactics in Rochdale.

Five Lamborghinis and one Mercedes G-Wagon were seized under Section 59 of the Police Reform Act 2002. In addition to the vehicle seizures, the drivers of the offending vehicles are facing prosecution for multiple driving offences.

Chief Inspector Danny Kabal of GMP’s TPACC stated, “We take road safety very seriously in GMP, and we will not tolerate careless, inconsiderate, anti-social or dangerous driving on our roads.” This operation highlights the police's commitment to ensuring safety on local roads and addressing the concerns of residents regarding reckless driving.

articles.title: Rochdale's Year as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture Generates Over £5.5 Million for Local Economy
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's designation as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture has resulted in more than £5.5 million in economic benefits, with over 213,000 attendees at nearly 300 events throughout the year.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture has proven to be a significant economic boost, generating over £5.5 million for the local economy, according to a recent report by Rochdale Council. The evaluation revealed that the borough attracted 213,099 attendees across 297 events during the 2025/2026 year, showcasing the cultural vibrancy of the area.

The report estimates that the average spend per visitor was around £25, although a separate assessment by Marketing Manchester suggested that daily visitor spending could be as high as £78. This indicates that the total economic impact could potentially reach £16.6 million, highlighting the success of the Town of Culture initiative.

Rochdale Council received £50,000 from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) Culture Fund to support various cultural activities from April 2025 to March 2026. Events such as 'The Herds', Street Eat, Rochdale Comedy Festival, Rochdale Pride, and the Ignite Fire Festival were among the highlights that attracted large crowds and contributed to the local economy.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation, expressed pride in the achievements of the year, noting that 94 per cent of attendees felt the events positively enhanced Rochdale's image. The council plans to build on this momentum by continuing to host significant cultural events in the future, aiming to further engage diverse communities and enhance the borough's reputation.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the little local verb 'cruckle': what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdalians still cling to it.
articles.summary: A short guide to the little local verb 'cruckle': what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdalians still cling to it.
articles.body:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” In everyday local speech cruckle is used to mean going over on, or twisting, the ankle — that awkward stumble you can usually walk off but that still makes you wince. This modern, conversational sense is widely reported in contemporary accounts of Rochdale speech. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

But cruckle is not a recent invention. Late nineteenth‑century dialect lexicography records an older verb crookle (also seen spelled crookle/crockle/cruckle in some sources) meaning “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble.” That semantic field — bending, limping, or hobbling — easily covers both the older senses and the narrow modern one about rolling an ankle. The English Dialect Dictionary compiled by Joseph Wright is the principal historical source for this family of forms. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

How did crookle become locally recognisable as cruckle in Rochdale? Dialect historians point to ordinary sound‑change and word‑formation processes: the base crook (a bend or hook) plus a frequentative/diminutive suffix ‑le (a familiar pattern in northern and Midland English) produces a verb meaning ‘to bend repeatedly or slightly’ — crook → crookle → cruckle in pronunciation. Comparative work on Germanic dialects shows related forms (kreukelen, krökeln, etc.), which helps explain the family’s meaning and shape. In short, cruckle is best seen as a local survival and reflex of an older dialect verb‑group, preserved in local speech. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Popular feeling in the borough treats it as a Rochdale speciality, and perceptual‑dialect research supports that association: in a recent draw‑a‑map study of Greater Manchester, respondents repeatedly used words and keywords tied to Rochdale — the authors include cruckle among locally salient labels that people use when describing the town’s speech. That is, people in the region identify cruckle as a Rochdale‑flavour word, even if closely related forms were recorded historically across parts of Lancashire and neighbouring counties. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

What does dialect research tell us beyond etymology and perception? Two points matter. First, folk‑linguistic studies show that local pride and visibility keep words alive: when people point to a term as “our word,” its social value rises and its use is reinforced across generations. Second, dialect atlases and historical dictionaries reveal that many words that now feel highly local had wider past distributions; what looks exclusive today can be the last local stronghold of a once broader regional term. In other words, cruckle’s apparent Rochdale exclusivity is as much about social identity and perception as it is about unique etymology. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

So what should Rochdalians take from this? Cruckle is a neat example of how small vocabulary items carry history and identity: its roots run into nineteenth‑century dialect lexicons and further back into Germanic patterns, while its present‑day life is shaped by local use and local recognition. It is not, strictly speaking, an invention only ever used inside the borough — historical records show kin‑forms elsewhere — but today it survives, thrives and signals “Rochdale” in the way only a handful of truly local words do. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a well-loved part of Healey Dell’s landscape — a place of geology, industry and storytelling rather than documented supernatural events.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a well-loved part of Healey Dell’s landscape — a place of geology, industry and storytelling rather than documented supernatural events.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel is one of those local names that makes you slow your pace on the riverside path and look twice. The spot — a narrow gorge where the River Spodden squeezes through a cleft called the Thrutch — has been admired for centuries because the water-worn rock can take on shapes that, with a little imagination, suggest a pulpit, bench and alcove. The Dell itself is an established nature reserve and visitor attraction, with a heritage centre, tea rooms and family trails. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The most concrete, documented facts are straightforward. Healey Dell is managed and promoted as a nature reserve by the borough and its industrial archaeology — mill sites, lodges and a striking Victorian railway viaduct — is part of the site’s real history. The viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England (list entry 1317784). That history of mills and railways explains why the Dell became a popular Victorian beauty spot and why writers and guidebooks have long pointed to the peculiar rock features there. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The “Fairies’ Chapel” name and the other colourful stories attached to the Thrutch come from the region’s rich oral and printed tradition. The best-known version of the tale appears in John Roby’s 19th‑century collection Traditions of Lancashire, where Roby records romances about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, an enchanted chapel, the Fairy Queen and prophecies tied to Healey. These are literary‑folklore accounts: vivid, localised retellings that collectors like Roby shaped for Victorian readers. They are valuable as records of what people told and believed, but they are not documentary proof that supernatural events occurred. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Later local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre reprise Roby’s material and other regional legends — including stories that mix fairies, witches and a fairy king — and they explain the physical origin of the name: erosive action by the river produced a cavernous niche that looked church‑like to observers. The centre also records local floods and landscape changes (for example an extreme storm on 4 July 1838 that altered sections of the Spodden valley), which helps explain why the rock features seen by earlier visitors are not exactly the same today. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

What can we say with reasonable certainty, and what is pure folklore? Facts: the place‑name and rock feature are real; Healey Dell’s industrial remains and railway viaduct are documented and protected; the site has been a site of local tourism since Victorian times. Legends: the tales of a Fairy King turning witches to stone, of prophetic fairy queens or of Robin Hood connections are elements of local storytelling preserved in collections like Roby’s and in later retellings — entertaining and culturally important, but unsupported by independent historical evidence. If a claim cannot be verified in archival records or contemporary sources, it should be treated as folklore. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

If you visit Healey Dell today, bring two pairs of eyes: one for the geology, mill ruins and the listed viaduct that really are there; the other for the stories people have told around that landscape for 150‑plus years. The Fairies’ Chapel is best enjoyed as a meeting place of nature, industrial history and imagination — a reminder that some places are important precisely because they gather stories as well as stones. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Secures 3-0 Victory Against Shrewsbury Town
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC achieved their first win of the season with a convincing 3-0 victory against Shrewsbury Town at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday evening, moving off the bottom of League Two.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC celebrated their first win of the season with a resounding 3-0 victory against Shrewsbury Town at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday evening, 1st September 2026. This win marks a significant turnaround for the team, who had struggled in their previous matches since returning to the English Football League (EFL).

The home side took control of the match early on, with Kane Taylor's cross nearly resulting in a goal when Dajaune Brown's header skimmed the crossbar. Rochdale opened the scoring in the 33rd minute when Baba Adeeko capitalised on a blocked shot from Emmanuel Dieseruvwe, slotting the ball past Shrewsbury goalkeeper Will Brook. Just before half-time, Luke Hannant doubled the lead, finishing expertly after a defensive error from Shrewsbury.

In the second half, Rochdale maintained their dominance, with Joe Gbode coming close to extending the lead. The third goal came in the 80th minute when substitute Jonny Smith raced through and curled a shot into the net, sealing a convincing win for the home side. This victory not only boosts Rochdale's morale but also lifts them off the bottom of League Two, providing a much-needed confidence boost as they look to build on this performance in upcoming matches.

Shrewsbury Town's manager, Gavin Cowan, expressed his disappointment with his team's performance, stating they were 'devoid of any desire to win' and struggled to create scoring opportunities despite having 16 shots throughout the match. Cowan's criticism highlights the challenges facing Shrewsbury as they aim to improve after suffering three defeats in four league matches. The result leaves Rochdale looking forward to their next fixtures with renewed hope.
